title: Federated Digital Twin-Driven Foundation Models for Energy-Aware Scheduling in Edge Data Centers.
abstract: The rapid deployment of foundation models and AI workloads has significantly increased the energy demand of modern data centers, particularly under edge computing environments characterized by limited resources, heterogeneous devices, and intermittent connectivity. This paper proposes a novel federated digital twin-driven framework for energy-aware scheduling and resilience enhancement in edge data centers. The proposed system integrates digital twin modeling, federated learning, and distributed energy-aware optimization to enable privacy-preserving, scalable, and adaptive model training across multiple edge nodes. To address challenges in communication efficiency, heterogeneity, and system robustness, we introduce a Double Robust Federated Learning (DRFL) architecture that incorporates blockchain-based trust management and distributionaware node selection. Experimental analysis demonstrates that the proposed framework improves energy efficiency, scheduling stability, and system resilience while preserving data privacy. This work highlights a cross-layer design paradigm for federated foundation models operating under resource-constrained edge environments.

title: Lucid: Lidar-Based Uav Classification and Detection for Airspace Surveillance.
abstract: Misuse of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) has surged dramatically in recent years, particularly in warfare and terrorism. These UAVs are small, and often operate at nights, making them challenging to detect solely using radar or vision-based surveillance systems. To address this concern, we propose Lucid, a LiDAR-based UAV detection system designed to identify fastmoving UAVs even in complex environments. Lucid distinguish UAVs from other objects by analyzing their unique mobility characteristics using spatio-temporal background subtraction, flying object extraction, flight trajectory estimation, and point cloud fusion techniques. We conduct extensive real-world LiDAR measurements using three different types and sizes of UAVs at four distinct environments to obtain 3D point cloud datasets of flight trajectories, and evaluate Lucid to demonstrate that it can reliably detect and distinguish UAVs from other flying objects such as birds with 96.39% accuracy. Lucid offers a practical and effective approach for detection of UAV threats, and can be used together with existing surveillance systems to address the growing concerns over UAV misuse.

title: Falconf: Configuration Error Diagnosis via Log Sequence Learning and Automated Misconfiguration Injections.
abstract: Misconfigurations are a leading cause of software failures, often manifesting as silent errors missed by conventional syntax checkers or absent in runtime logs. Diagnosing misconfigurations remains a hard problem despite multiple attempts over the years to address it. Although recent Large Language Model (LLM) based learning techniques open up new promising directions, these are limited by the existence of explicit indicators or explanatory contents of the failure. In this paper, we present Falconf- a log-based deep learning framework for misconfiguration diagnosis. It is built on the hypothesis that even when logs do not directly reveal the cause of failure, the sequence of log events contains latent patterns that reflect the nature of the underlying misconfiguration. To capture these log-flow patterns, we train a transformer model atop logs generated using automated fault injection on the target software's configuration space. During inference, given a failure log from the misconfigured software, Falconf produces a ranked list of likely misconfigured configuration parameters. Our evaluation on 3 distributed software shows Falconf is highly effective in misconfiguration diagnosis, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM-based techniques by at least 46.9%, while achieving an average Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.95 over the 3 software.

title: AURORA-Q: Asynchronous Unified Resource Optimizer for Quantum Simulation on HPC System.
abstract: This paper presents AURORA-Q, a tiered-memory quantum circuit simulation framework designed to overcome the memory bottleneck and scalability limits of large-scale quantum circuit simulation on Perlmutter. Its primary strategy is to extend beyond GPU-centric designs bounded by VRAM and introduce a unified tiered-memory architecture that integrates GPU VRAM, DRAM, and storage into a simulation framework. With this design, AURORA-Q partitions the full state vector into subsets, manages their residency across memory tiers, overlaps computation with data movement through an async execution pipeline, and employs a dynamic two-level cache with adaptive resource control to exploit access locality under constrained resources. Our evaluation demonstrates that AURORA-Q executes up to 43 qubit simulations on 512 GPUs, a scale unattainable by existing state-of-the-art simulators due to limited memory resources. AURORA-Q achieves up to$2.91 \times$speedup compared to baselines, while maintaining up to a 79.3% cache hit rate and reducing pipeline stalls by 73% to hide I/O latency.

title: Reliable Federated Fine-Tuning for Multilingual ASR.
abstract: Cross-silo federated ASR fine-tuning can improve multilingual services in settings such as hospitals, emergency call centers, and government help desks without centralizing audio data. Under heterogeneous client distributions, however, standard aggregation may improve average performance while leaving a persistent tail of high-error silos. At the same time, large pretrained ASR backbones make full-parameter updates expensive, motivating mechanisms that improve tail reliability under tight per-round training and communication budgets. We present TiRA-FL, a federated fine-tuning method that combines hypernetwork-generated low-rank adapters with explicit updateinteraction control. TiRA-FL maintains shared and tail adapter branches, uses EMA-smoothed validation risk to identify highrisk clients, and applies a cosine gate during aggregation. Aligned tail updates enter the shared branch to propagate compatible gains, while misaligned updates remain protected in the tail branch to limit negative transfer. Experiments on FLEURS with a wav2vec2-based MMS-1B ASR model and CTC fine-tuning report mean performance and tail reliability using distributional client metrics, including p95 and worst-client CER/WER, under fixed participation, training, and communication budgets.

title: Hash-Based Asynchronous MVBA with Optimal Complexity and Near-Optimal Resilience.
abstract: Multi-valued validated Byzantine agreement (MVBA), a fundamental primitive of distributed computing, allows$n$processes to agree on a valid$\ell$-bit value, despite$t$faulty processes behaving maliciously. Among hashbased solutions for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults, the state-of-the-art HMVBA protocol (DSN'25) achieves optimal$O\left(n^{2}\right)$message complexity, (near-)optimal$O\left(n \ell+n^{2} \lambda \log n\right)$bit complexity, and optimal$O(1)$time complexity. However, it only tolerates$t<\frac{1}{5} n$failures. In contrast, the best-known optimally-resilient protocol, SQ (S&P'25), incurs a higher bit complexity of$O\left(n^{2} \ell+\right.\ n^{3} \lambda)$. This poses a fundamental theoretical question: Can a hash-based protocol be designed for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults that simultaneously achieves optimal asymptotic complexity and optimal resilience? This paper takes a significant step toward answering the question. Namely, we introduce Reducer++, an MVBA protocol that tolerates up to$t<\left(\frac{1}{3}-\epsilon\right) n$adaptive failures, for any fixed constant$\epsilon>0$. The design of Reducer++ leverages hash functions modeled as random oracles to realize a random permutation abstraction, which is then used to guarantee termination in constant time. This yields an MVBA protocol with constant time complexity, quadratic message complexity, and quasi-quadratic bit complexity, with constants dependent on$\epsilon$.

title: Silent Data Corruption in Distributed Genai-Augmented Data Pipelines: An Empirical Study of Hallucination-Induced Failure Propagation.
abstract: Enterprise data pipelines increasingly integrate generative AI (GenAI) components for information extraction, transformation, and analytics. Unlike traditional infrastructure failures, hallucinated outputs from large language models introduce semantic errors that remain structurally valid but factually incorrect, allowing them to bypass conventional validation mechanisms. This paper conceptualizes such failures as a form of Silent Data Corruption (SDC) occurring at the semantic layer of GenAIaugmented data pipelines. We empirically evaluate corruption propagation across multi-stage pipelines and introduce three quantitative measures: hallucination base rate (H), reasoning amplification factor (A), and structured distribution distortion (D). Controlled experiments using benchmark datasets and a chained pipeline demonstrate that hallucination-induced errors propagate through reasoning and classification layers and produce measurable downstream distortions in aggregate analytics without triggering structural validation failures. The results highlight the need for semantic observability and reliability mechanisms in distributed GenAI-integrated data systems

title: PR-Reduce: Heterogeneity-Aware Proportional Allreduce for Distributed Training.
abstract: Distributed Deep Learning (DDL) has become a core technique for training increasingly large and complex models. While parallelizing local training across workers improves scalability, DDL efficiency is often limited by stragglers. Recent studies have proposed partial-reduce schemes that fully or partially exclude slow workers. This, however, wastes their capacity and misses opportunities to improve model accuracy. To address this, we present PR-Reduce, a PRoportional Reduce communication framework that allows each worker to contribute gradient updates in proportion to its computing and communication resources. The key enabler of PR-Reduce is a selective compressive sensing (CS) design that allows encoding of any number of local gradients while ensuring reliable reconstruction of the true global average, even when each gradient is contributed by a different subset of workers. Simulations show that PR-Reduce better utilizes heterogeneous resources than partial-reduce, reducing gradient reconstruction error by up to 66.5% without harming model convergence. This benefit grows with greater heterogeneity, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating the straggler problem.

title: Data-Free Early Stopping for Federated Learning with Consensus of Local Task Vectors.
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training in a decentralized manner without sharing raw data. However, dependence on fixed global rounds in hyperparameter tuning wastes resources on 'bad' configurations that tend to diverge. To overcome this, we propose a data-free early stopping framework that terminates 'bad' configurations at early stages by monitoring the consensus of local task vectors, without accessing validation data. Numerical experiments on medical image classification tasks show that the proposed approach is comparable to validation-based early stopping across state-ofthe-art FL methods. In detail, our framework cuts off 'bad' configurations within 1.8% of the fixed-round budget on average.

title: Scene Complexity-Aware Adaptive Batch Separation for Robust Camera-based BEV Perception.
abstract: Accurate bird's-eye-view (BEV) map generation is essential for autonomous driving, yet camera-based methods often suffer from occlusions and limited depth perception. This study identifies that simultaneous processing of multiple camera images can lead to cross-sample feature contamination within neural networks, degrading map accuracy-especially in complex environments. To address this, we propose AutoGranularity, an adaptive framework designed to optimize the trade-off between perception accuracy and inference efficiency on resourceconstrained edge devices. AutoGranularity dynamically adjusts its image processing strategy based on a scene complexity score, which is calculated using three factors: object density, Shannon entropy, and spatial distribution. In complex scenes, the framework processes images using a sub-batch processing scheme based on scene-complexity-aware grouping to eliminate feature interference and enhance accuracy; in simpler scenarios, it employs standard batch processing to maintain real-time performance. Experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that our method maintains competitive Vehicle IoU performance even under occluded conditions. Notably, it alleviates approximately 18.75% of the inference time overhead introduced by a full sub-batch processing scheme, effectively balancing high-fidelity mapping with the real-time demands of autonomous driving.

title: Delay-Aware Robust Quantum Control for Overcoming Micro-Jitter in Modular Quantum Computing.
abstract: Modular quantum computing requires continuous pulse control to overcome physical constraints such as inter-node communication delay and amplitude damping. Traditional optimal control algorithms assume deterministic environments and fail catastrophically under nanoscale delay fluctuations, known as micro-jitter. To address this vulnerability, we propose a delayaware robust control framework utilizing a multi-dimensional minimax objective function. By simultaneously evaluating a probability distribution of delays within a realistic micro-jitter window, the framework autonomously synthesizes a single delayproof composite pulse. This approach prevents localized overfitting and naturally induces a decoupling mechanism to cancel phase errors. Coupled with a quantum speed limit (QSL) analysis to ensure adequate control duration, the proposed framework significantly improves worst-case fidelity, which provides a highly reliable pathway for deterministic entanglement generation in noisy distributed networks.

title: Spatio-Temporal Parallelism for Diffusion Model Inference on Heterogeneous Multi-GPU Systems.
abstract: The widespread adoption of diffusion models for image generation necessitates efficient parallel inference to manage their substantial computational overhead. However, current parallel inference paradigms primarily target homogeneous clusters, often failing to maintain high efficiency in realistic, heterogeneous multi-GPU environments where hardware disparities and fluctuating background workloads cause severe straggler effects. This paper introduces Orchestra, a robust framework that orchestrates fine-grained parallelism across both temporal and spatial dimensions to harmonize computational loads in such settings. Temporally, Orchestra employs a novel computation-aware step allocator using a tiered step reduction strategy, intelligently pruning denoising steps on slower devices after warmup phases and execution synchronization. Spatially, Orchestra performs an elastic patch parallelism mechanism which adaptively adjusts the spatial workload intensity by assigning non-uniform image patches tailored to GPUs according to their computational capability. Extensive experiments on load-imbalanced and heterogeneous clusters validate Orchestra's efficacy in mitigating performance bottlenecks. Compared to patch parallelism, a state-of-the-art diffusion inference framework, our method reduces end-to-end latency by up to 45% and significantly boosts resource utilization on heterogeneous GPUs.

title: Privacy-Preserving Chunk Scheduling in a BitTorrent Implementation of Federated Learning.
abstract: Decentralized mix-and-forward designs remove the server, but repeated local mixing can attenuate global information under heterogeneity and exposes peer-to-peer neighborhoods as a privacy attack surface. To preserve FedAvgstyle aggregation semantics (over updates reconstructable by the round deadline) while scaling dissemination, we present FLTorrent, a BitTorrent-based dissemination layer for serverless FL with a short warm-up. Warm-up hardens within-round source unlinkability—a dissemination-layer goal orthogonal to content protections (e.g., DP or secure aggregation)—via (i) pre-round obfuscation, (ii) randomized lags, and (iii) coordination-only non-owner-first scheduling (tracker off the data path), before switching to vanilla BitTorrent swarming. We upper-bound the per-transfer attribution posterior by the fraction of owner chunks in a sender's eligible cover set, and derive a tighter highprobability bound that improves with early non-owner mass. A simple heuristic, GreedyFastestFirst, attains$\approx 92 \%$of a bandwidth-optimal max-flow upper bound, while warm-up remains a stable$\approx 12 \%$share of a round across 100–500 peers. Under an observation-only local adversary, FLTorrent drives attribution success close to neighborhood-level random guessing for typical nodes, improves with network size, and remains robust under collusion. In LLM-scale dissemination stress tests over 7–10 Gbps access links, FLTorrent adds only$\sim {6}-{10} \%$round-time overhead relative to BitTorrent-only. Overall, FLTorrent shows that within-round unlinkability and BitTorrent-level efficiency can co-exist with predictable, low overheads at scale.

title: COAR: Computation-Aware Erasure-Coded Repair in Storage Clusters for Distributed Data Analytics.
abstract: Distributed data analytics clusters are widely used to process and store massive datasets. Erasure coding offers a cost-efficient mechanism for achieving data reliability, but incurs substantial bandwidth overhead for failure recovery. Most prior studies on erasure-coded repair focus on minimizing repair bandwidth. However, we observe that erasure-coded repair performance is affected not only by network bandwidth but also by the limited computational capacity under distributed data analytics workloads. We present COAR, a computation-aware erasure-coded repair scheme designed for storage clusters in distributed data analytics environments. COAR exploits the periodic computation patterns of analytics workloads to estimate repair computational capacity via the decoding throughput metric. It strategically assigns and schedules repair tasks by jointly considering computational and network resource states across nodes. Experiments conducted on Alibaba Cloud show that COAR reduces single-chunk, multi-chunk, and full-node repair time by up to$\mathbf{5 9. 8 0 \%, 5 8. 0 7 \%}$, and$\mathbf{5 9. 4 7 \%}$, respectively, compared with existing repair schemes under diverse analytics workloads.

title: QCLink: Offloading Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computation to SmartNICs via RDMA.
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms rely on tight iterative control loops that alternate between quantum evaluations and classical parameter updates. Despite recent efforts on accelerating quantum execution and real-time control paths, the endto-end performance of these workloads is often bottlenecked by the distributed control plane, where iterations incur frequent finegrained message exchanges, host CPU mediation, and amplified tail latency. In this paper, we take a networking perspective on hybrid quantum-classical computing and show that the classical optimization loop constitutes a key scalability barrier. We present QCLInk (Quantum-Classical Link), a SmartNICassisted offloading framework that moves hybrid optimization into the network data plane and leverages RDMA to enable low-latency, CPU-bypassed communication between classical controllers and quantum backends. By executing parameter perturbation, gradient estimation, and iteration control directly on the SmartNIC, QCLINK turns hybrid optimization into a data-plane service, reducing per-iteration overhead and mitigating controlloop jitter. We implement a prototype of QCLInk with SmartNICresident optimization logic and RDMA-based messaging primitives. Experiments demonstrate that QCLINK significantly improves per-iteration latency and end-to-end completion time over hostcentric baselines, while stabilizing tail latency and freeing host CPU resources under concurrent workloads.

title: FedRFF: Enhanced Federated Random Fourier Feature Framework for IoT Anomaly Detection.
abstract: The rapid growth of IoT devices poses immense challenges for distributed anomaly detection, especially under privacy constraints, heterogeneous data distributions, and limited communication resources. To address these issues, this paper proposes FedRFF, a novel federated unsupervised anomaly detection framework that integrates random Fourier features (RFF) with adaptive momentum alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) optimization. FedRFF achieves kernel space approximation to capture nonlinear global feature structures, enabling cross-device anomaly learning without labeled data or raw data sharing. Two algorithms are developed under FedRFF: FedRE (Euclidean space) for smooth global consensus feature embedding, and FedRG (Grassmann manifold) for modeling device-specific subspace structures via Riemannian projection/retraction, enhancing representation and generalization for complex manifold features. An adaptive ADMM mechanism dynamically adjusts penalty parameters and dual step sizes based on local gradient history, eliminating manual tuning. A momentum aggregation strategy mitigates non-IID data-induced client drift using exponential moving averages of local parameters. Extensive experiments on UNSW-NB15 and TON IoT datasets demonstrate that FedRFF outperforms state-of-the-art federated anomaly detection methods in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, verifying its practicality for real-world IoT anomaly detection.

title: A Cyber-Physical Cooperative Scheme for Energy Scheduling and Dynamic Pricing in Charging Station Alliances via Cloud-Edge Intelligence.
abstract: Coordinating geographically dispersed PhotovoltaicEnergy Storage Charging Stations (PSCSs) constitutes a complex Cyber-Physical System (CPS) characterized by the tight coupling of physical energy flows and cyber information exchanges. However, the efficient operation of this CPS is challenged by the stochasticity of Electric Vehicle (EV) demand, the intermittency of renewable energy, and the inherent tendency toward monopoly pricing in fully cooperative settings. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a cyber-physical cooperative control scheme for the Charging Station Alliance (CSA) utilizing a Cloud-Edge collaborative framework based on Centralized Training and Distributed Execution (CTDE). First, a Markov game model is formulated in which PSCSs operate as fully cooperative Internet of Things (IoT) edge agents. To curb irrational monopoly pricing behaviors, an Inverse Demand Function (IDF) is integrated with a gravity-based attraction model to explicitly quantify EV user sensitivity to charging prices and spatial distance. Second, a Cosine Annealing-based Multi-Agent Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (CA-MATD3) algorithm is proposed. This architecture enables lightweight edge inference to overcome communication latency constraints while leveraging cloud resources for global policy optimization. By dynamically adjusting learning rates, CA-MATD3 effectively mitigates nonstationarity in dynamic IoT environments. Extensive simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme prevents excessive price hikes, and CA-MATD3 outperforms benchmark algorithms by$\mathbf{1. 3 \% - 3 8. 6 \%}$in terms of overall profit under various scenarios.

title: Prism: Proactive Workload-Aware Optimization for Hybrid-Service in LMaaS Systems.
abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) in interactive and content-generation applications, Language-Model-as-a-Service (LMaaS) platforms have become essential infrastructure. However, existing resource provisioning and request scheduling strategies are fundamentally limited in handling hybrid-service workloads in LMaaS, leading to inefficient resource utilization and violations of Service Level Objectives (SLOs). To tackle these challenges, we propose Prism, a proactive workload-aware optimization framework for hybridservice in LMaaS. Motivated by insights from traces analysis, Prism introduces a novel Periodic Planning-Online Scheduling-Adaptive Tuning (POA) paradigm that integrates two key mechanisms. First, a provision-revision mechanism combines long-term forecasting with fine-grained runtime adjustments to maintain responsiveness and resource efficiency. Second, a two-level heterogeneity-aware scheduling mechanism coordinates inter-instance routing and intra-instance batching based on realtime request profiling to reduce latency and enhance goodput. Extensive evaluations show that Prism reduces tail latency by up to 63.9%, mitigates 85.7% of SLO violations, and improves goodput by 52.8%, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while sustaining high GPU utilization.

title: GALUPA: Gossiping Aggregated Locking and Output Proofs for Accountability in BFT.
abstract: Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) protocols are essential for ensuring consistency in decentralized systems. However, once safety is violated, accountability becomes crucial for identifying malicious replicas. Existing accountable BFT protocols often rely on external observers or incur up to$O\left(N^{4}\right)$communication overhead due to broadcast-based mechanisms. We propose GALUPA, a decentralized accountability mechanism that detects Byzantine misbehavior by leveraging conflicting Quorum Certificates (QCs) exchanged solely among replicas. Compatible with PBFT, HotStuff, and BFT-SMaRt, GALUPA uses a randomized gossip protocol to disseminate aggregated signed locking information. We develop a probabilistic model based on Erdós-Rényi random graphs (ERG) to analyze the accountability success rate under varying network sizes and parameter configurations. Our analysis shows that GALUPA introduces only$O(k N)$message complexity for any fixed target success rate. We implement GALUPA on the BFT-SMaRt platform and evaluate its performance in networks of up to 160 replicas. Experimental results show that GALUPA maintains over 70% throughput while achieving 99.9999% accountability success,$8 \times$higher than that of the broadcast-based baseline.

title: HPC-VQPU: Exporting Device-Aware Quantum Simulation From Batch-Scheduled HPC as an Interactive Service.
abstract: GPU-Accelerated quantum simulation is essential for NISQ-era research, but the HPC systems best suited to these workloads expose an operating model oriented toward security and scheduling. That model is poorly aligned with the interactive, device-oriented workflows expected by quantum software. We present HPC-vQPU, a two-plane architecture that exports HPC-hosted simulation as a virtual-QPU service without weakening the site's security posture. A cloud-facing control plane exposes a device-oriented REST API for circuit submission, lifecycle tracking, and event streaming; an unprivileged loginnode agent polls outward, atomically claims tasks, and dispatches scheduler-backed GPU work. A topology-and calibration-Aware device snapshot is bound at claim time and carried into each GPU job as a self-contained input, decoupling execution from live server contact while preserving calibration fidelity across scheduling delay. Deployed on Pawsey's Setonix supercomputer with NVIDIA Grace Hopper nodes, Qiskit-Aer/cuQuantum, and real IBM Fez calibration data for a 156-qubit heavy-hex device, HPC-vQPU adds only 2.0-3.4 s of interface-visible overhead in our deployment (3.4-5.9% of end-To-end latency) for 28-32 qubit circuits. The bound snapshot measurably changes output distributions, device state is fixed at claim rather than submission time, and task lifecycle consistency is preserved through agent failure and multi-Agent contention without privileged deployment or firewall changes.

title: LSCFL: Clustered Federated Learning with Label Semantics for Label-Skewed Non-IID Data.
abstract: Federated learning often suffers from severe performance degradation and unstable convergence when clients' data are highly non-independent and non-identically distributed. This paper proposes Clustered Federated Learning with Label Semantics (LSCFL), which constructs semantic client identity vectors from label information and performs clustering to form groups of clients with similar data distributions. Clustering is carried out in a pre-training stage based solely on these identity vectors, without requiring a pre-specified number of clusters or access to model parameters or gradients. Experiments under two challenging non-IID settings show that LSCFL accurately recovers latent client clusters, and outperforms baselines significantly on complex tasks with accuracy gains ranging from 0.61% to 59.23%. Furthermore, LSCFL maintains computational time comparable to FedAvg, reduces per-round training time by 3.45% to 53.18% compared to other non-IID FL methods, and remains robust with increased local steps. We further provide an optional differential privacy mechanism, in which adding Gaussian noise to client identity vectors offers tunable privacy levels, making LSCFL suitable for privacy-sensitive applications.

title: BCD-Megatron: A Cost-Effective Training System for Large Language Models.
abstract: Training large language models typically demands substantial GPU memory and significant financial investment, posing a major barrier for many small-to-medium research groups and companies. In this paper, we present a full-parameter pretraining and fine-tuning framework, BCD-Megatron, built on a block-wise update strategy, together with a set of engineering optimizations, enabling efficient model training on both lowcost consumer GPUs (e.g., RTX 4090) and high-performance computing clusters. By partitioning model parameters into blocks and updating only a subset of parameters in each training iteration, our approach markedly reduces the GPU memory requirement. Experimental results show that, under the same hardware configuration, our method reduces the training cost of a 7B-parameter model to 33% of that required by conventional fullparameter training on high-end clusters (A100/A800). Moreover, despite the substantial cost reduction, our approach achieves comparable wall-clock training time and accuracy to traditional methods. This progress significantly lowers the hardware barrier to large-scale model development and demonstrates the practicality and cost-effectiveness of full-parameter training using low-cost GPU clusters.

title: On Hierarchical Caching with Delayed Hits.
abstract: Designing caching algorithms to minimize aggregate latency is a long-standing challenge in memory-intensive and latency-sensitive computer systems. This challenge is further exacerbated by a recently discovered phenomenon, known as delayed hits, which renders traditional optimal algorithms unable to guarantee minimal latency. To bridge this gap, this paper pioneers a comprehensive algorithmic analysis for hierarchical caching with delayed hits. First, we analytically establish a competitiveness lower bound for any online caching algorithm. Second, we introduce a novel online algorithm that synthesizes two key technical innovations: an enhanced marking policy that executes separate marking processes for different cache layers, and a heuristic ranking function that leverages historical request patterns to prioritize items based on their estimated aggregate latency per cache miss. Finally, we theoretically prove that the proposed algorithm can asymptotically match the lower bound under some mild conditions. Extensive experiments validate its effectiveness and superiority over state-of-the-art solutions.

title: cGraph: A Compact and Efficient Graph-Based Index for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search.
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is critical for high-dimensional data retrieval. While graph-based indexes deliver state-of-the-art accuracy and throughput, they incur prohibitive memory overhead by storing both graph topology and full-precision vectors. Complementary to out-ofcore methods, we propose cGraph, a compact graph-based index structure for approximate nearest neighbor search. Our method introduces super-nodes, a novel structure that compresses both graph topology and full-precision vectors. We develop a twostage search algorithm for efficient nearest neighbor queries on this structure, along with both static and dynamic construction algorithms. These enable transformation of existing graph indices into our new structure and support dynamic operations including insertions and deletions. Our comprehensive evaluations show that cGraph reduces memory consumption by up to 60% while preserving high recall, incurs less than 5% throughput penalty, and delivers consistent performance when compressing indexes from both Hnswlib and DiskANN, demonstrating its scalability and versatility for large-scale ANNS.

title: Efficient Deployment of Lightweight LLMs on Edge Devices: Kernel-Level Profiling and Cross-Platform Insights.
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in real-time edge scenarios, their efficient deployment on heterogeneous, resource-constrained devices becomes a critical challenge. However, the diversity of model architectures, hardware platforms, and inference frameworks complicates performance prediction and optimization. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of seven lightweight LLMs across four representative edge platforms, including the MacBook Pro, Jetson Orin NX, Jetson AGX Orin, and an edge server with a desktop GPU. The evaluation focuses on key metrics such as model load time, token-level inference latency (TPOT and TTFT), memory usage, power dissipation, and semantic output relevance. Moreover, this paper explores hardware-specific bottlenecks such as memory-bound operations and inefficient kernel execution by using fine-grained profiling tools. The analysis reveals significant performance variation across model-hardware combinations, highlighting the importance of model selection and optimization techniques, including operator fusion and cross-platform insights. These findings offer practical guidance for deploying LLMs efficiently in real-world edge environments.

title: Predicate-Agnostic Filtered ANNS for Low-Selectivity Hybrid Queries in FAISS.
abstract: Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (Filtered ANNS) has become a cornerstone for modern production systems, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and recommendation systems, which require simultaneous vector similarity search and structured attribute filtering. In this paper, to address the navigation failures in predicate-agnostic Filtered ANNS under low-selectivity constraints, we propose BRIDGE (Bucket-Reinforced Indexing for Dual Graph Enhancement). While traditional graph or partition-based methods suffer from fragmented search paths or inefficient scope identification, BRIDGE introduces a hybrid architecture to restore logical connectivity. We develop two synergistic strategies: BRIDGE_A for adaptive centroid probing and BRIDGE_B for cluster-assisted traversal. Evaluations on datasets of up to 10M vectors show that BRIDGE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including NaviX and ACORN, in both recall and throughput. Implemented as a native FAISS extension, BRIDGE provides a robust, production-ready solution for high-performance hybrid vector search.

title: Accelerating Cold Starts of On-Device LLMs via Multi-Source Inference-Aware Parameter Loading.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed on edge devices suffer from severe cold-start latency, making time to first token (TTFT) the primary determinant of user-perceived responsiveness. On resource-constrained edge platforms, TTFT is dominated by model parameter loading. Limited local storage bandwidth and mmap-based lazy paging significantly delay bringing model weights into memory, even though faster network links are often available. To address this, we present CoLLM, a multisource and inference-aware loading framework that accelerates cold starts for on-device LLMs. CoLLM replaces page-faultdriven loading with an explicit, inference-aware I/O manager that aggregates bandwidth from local storage and neighboring edge devices, and overlaps parameter loading with inference execution. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, CoLLM further prioritizes the on-demand loading of activated experts to avoid unnecessary I/O. We implement CoLLM on llama.cpp and evaluate it on a real-world edge testbed. Across multiple dense and MoE LLMs under cold-start conditions, CoLLM improves parameter loading throughput by$\mathbf{1. 6 4} \boldsymbol{\times} \mathbf{- 2. 1 0} \boldsymbol{\times}$and reduces TTFT by$43-82 \%$, demonstrating that collaboratively and inferenceaware loading model parameters from neighboring edge devices effectively overcomes cold-start latency. Our implementation is released as open source.

title: GMACAuth: Generative Continuous Authentication via Memory-Augmented Causal Attention.
abstract: With the widespread adoption of mobile devices, secure user authentication has become increasingly critical. Traditional mechanisms, such as passwords and graphical patterns, are easy to deploy but vulnerable to attacks and cannot provide continuous verification throughout a session. As a result, sensor-based continuous authentication using behavioral biometrics captured by motion sensors, such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers, has gained significant attention. Despite this progress, most existing systems rely on classificationbased or reconstruction-based models. The former rely on compressed features optimized solely for distinguishing training samples and therefore suffer from information loss, which limits their generalization to unseen attacks. The latter often reconstruct both legitimate and impostor inputs with similar fidelity, resulting in reconstruction errors that are insufficiently discriminative for threshold-based decisions. To address these limitations, we propose GMACAuth, a generative continuous authentication framework driven by memory-augmented causal attention (MACA). MACA leverages a user-specific memory bank to constrain autoregressive next-timestep prediction over multisensor sequences to the legitimate behavioral subspace. During authentication, GMACAuth encodes real-time sensor data, generates next-timestep predictions via MACA, and compares them with the actual observed sequence, accepting the user only when the similarity exceeds a predefined threshold. We further introduce a threshold-aware contrastive authentication loss that directly incorporates the authentication threshold into the training objective, enforcing legitimate similarities to remain above the decision boundary while suppressing impostor similarities below it. Experimental results on our dataset show that GMACAuth achieves 98.90% accuracy and 1.64% EER with 70 unseen users, demonstrating strong robustness in open-set scenarios.

title: Chimera: An Efficient Multimodal Embodied Inference Framework with Complexity-Aware Edge-Cloud Routing.
abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal language models (MLMs) have empowered embodied agents with sophisticated task planning in a variety of smart scenarios such as smart household. However, achieving high-quality responses while maintaining low end-to-end (E2E) latency across heterogeneous tasks remains a critical challenge. Simple commands (e.g., emergency stop) demand millisecond-level responses, which are best served by edge-deployed MLMs. While complex long-horizon planning requires cloud-based reasoning, creating a fundamental tension between computational resources and timing constraints. Existing solutions fail to address this duality due to: 1) inadequate ability of handling multi-modal inputs, 2) static resource allocation ignoring task complexity heterogeneity, and 3) weak scalability faced with dynamic model deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose Chimera, an innovative multi-modal embodied inference framework with complexity-aware edgecloud routing that features: 1) a lightweight complexity predictor estimating high-level sub-task counts from multi-modal inputs, 2) an adaptive retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism that scales context retrieval by task complexity, and 3) a dynamic complexity-driven routing optimized for latency-quality tradeoff. Extensive evaluations on prevalent benchmarks show that Chimera outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 78.04% reduction in E2E latency and 17.18% improvement in response quality while enabling plug-and-play MLM scalability.

title: Enabling Realtime Stream Processing with Partial Computation Offloading.
abstract: Real-time stream processing is fundamental to IoT applications, yet existing stream processing engines typically deploy jobs monolithically either at the edge or in the cloud, overlooking opportunities for fine-grained computation offloading. Recent edge-cloud collaborative approaches improve flexibility by optimizing operator placement, but they still treat operators as indivisible units and rely on binary offloading decisions, incurring substantial state transfer and scheduling overhead. In this paper, we propose an iterative operator abstraction that decouples operator execution across the edge and the cloud, enabling partial computation at the edge while forwarding intermediate results for cloud-side processing. By overlapping computation and data transmission, this abstraction unlocks new optimization opportunities beyond binary deployment. Building on this idea, we present Elink, a dependency-aware partial offloading framework for large-scale IoT stream processing. Elink combines an operator abstraction module, a dynamic deployment optimizer, and an elastic incremental stream orchestrator to jointly address complex operator dependencies, continuous partitioning decisions, and dynamic network conditions. The optimizer decomposes the resulting high-complexity optimization problem to ensure logical consistency and computational efficiency, while the orchestrator supports lightweight, incremental state migration with low overhead. We implement Elink on Apache Flink and evaluate it with large-scale real-world traces from the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge and RIoTBench. Results show Elink reduces the end-to-end latency by 20.4% compared to state-of-the-art methods

title: ZeroSwap: A Practical Solution to the Double Swapping Problem in Virtualized Environments.
abstract: Memory overcommitment is a fundamental technique in cloud computing that enables providers to maximize resource utilization by allocating more memory to virtual machines than physically available on the host. However, this practice introduces a critical performance anomaly known as double swapping, where both the host and guest independently swap the same memory pages to disk, resulting in redundant I/O operations. This paper introduces ZEROSWAP, a lightweight coordination mechanism that eliminates double swapping. ZEROSWAP intercepts guest I/O operations and distinguishes between normal disk writes, which must be preserved for data consistency, and swaprelated writes that are candidates for optimization. ZEROSWAP requires no modifications to guest operating systems and imposes negligible overhead. We evaluated ZEROSWAP on modern datacenter hardware configurations, including high-speed SSDs and disaggregated storage architectures, using workloads from NPB, SPEC CPU2017, and Memcached. Our results demonstrate that ZE-ROSWAP achieves application speedups of up to 7.06×.

title: Distributed Variational Quantum Optimisation by Entanglement-Selective Transport.
abstract: Distributed quantum optimisation is challenging because computing the problem cost function across multiple quantum processors requires non-local gates, which can incur overhead in latency and fidelity. Here we introduce QESTO, a distributed variational ansatz for graph-based discrete optimisation that requires only persistent pre-shared Bell pairs for remote operations. Using local operations, it encodes local constraint information in the Bell pairs that is leveraged to produce amplitude transfer towards globally valid distributed solution states. QESTO requires one Bell pair per distributed edge of the problem graph and, after initialisation of the Bell states, uses no non-local gates. On two bounded weighted Wang tile-matching problem ensembles, QESTO achieves stronger convergence to low-cost tilings than equivalently partitioned QAOA with no distributed gates at ansatz depths of two or higher, and exceeds the mean performance of monolithic QAOA at the deepest studied depth in both ensembles. These results suggest that persistent entanglement can support useful variational communication while reducing per-layer nonlocal gate overhead.

title: PARS: Optimizing High-Dimensional Vector Search with Dimensional Reduction and Ray Tracing Core.
abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search in high-dimensional spaces is a fundamental but challenging problem. GPU-based graph indexes have recently emerged as a promising solution. However, such methods have a large memory footprint and are memory-bandwidth bound when operating on high-dimensional vectors, which limits their scalability on commodity GPUs. In this paper, we propose PARS, a GPU-based ANN search method that improves both efficiency and scalability through dimensionality reduction. PARS projects data points into a low-dimensional space using principal component analysis (PCA), where distance relationships are sufficiently preserved for computation. We further design a sampling-based method to determine the minimum projection dimension required to meet a target recall. To improve the search performance, we leverage the emerging RT cores to identify high-quality entry points. Additionally, we introduce an optional GPU buffer that dynamically supplies full-precision vectors for each query batch, improving search accuracy under tight memory constraints. Experiments on a wide range of datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of PARS. At$\mathbf{9 0 \% - 9 5 \%}$recall, PARS achieves up to$\mathbf{9. 3} \times$speedup over CAGRA, the current GPU-based state of the art, while reducing GPU memory usage by$\mathbf{2 3. 1 \% - 7 3. 0 \%}$, enabling ANN search on 100M-scale datasets using a single NVIDIA L40 GPU.

title: Signet: Scalable Network-Driven Proof of Notification for Blockchain Systems.
abstract: In blockchain systems, event notification is a valuable feature that eliminates the need for clients to actively monitor each event recorded by the blockchain. However, providing proof of notification-a verifiable guarantee that a notification was sent-is challenging to scale in high-throughput environments. This paper presents Signet, a novel system that enables the network itself to provide scalable and verifiable proof of notification. Leveraging path-aware networks, Signet utilizes Autonomous Systems (ASes) along the agreed-upon traffic path as impartial witnesses. These ASes, relied upon by both the notifier and recipient, provide lightweight proofs of packet observation to be submitted to the blockchain. This approach minimizes computational overhead and storage costs while maintaining security and scalability. Our evaluation demonstrates that the routers can handle over a million notifications per second per core, with under a microsecond of per-packet overhead, and that the smart contract operations on the blockchain incur negligible costs.

title: A Meta Stopping Mechanism for a KD-Based Decentralized System.
abstract: Decentralized knowledge distillation has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative learning across distributed nodes while keeping data local. However, most existing approaches rely on fixed communication schedules or a predetermined number of training rounds, which can lead to unnecessary communication and computation after performance gains have saturated. In this paper, we propose a meta-stopping mechanism for decentralized knowledge distillation that adaptively terminates collaboration based on local and cross-client validation signals. The proposed framework combines patience-, divergence-, and convergence-based criteria to detect when further distillation is no longer beneficial. We evaluate the approach on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST under highly non-i.i.d. data distributions. Results show that the proposed stopping strategies substantially reduce communication cost while preserving competitive accuracy, achieving favorable trade-offs between efficiency and predictive performance.

title: Graph Attention-Based Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Low-Latency Reliable Task Replication in Mobile Edge Computing.
abstract: In distributed Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) systems, task replication enhances reliability by duplicating offloaded tasks across multiple Base Stations (BS), mitigating disruptions from user mobility, server failures, and network dynamics. Nevertheless, redundant replicas consume scarce computational and bandwidth resources, thereby elevating total latency in constrained MEC environments. Existing replication methods are often driven by independent local-threshold triggers or rely on unrealistic assumptions of timely global state visibility, under partial observability and coupled resources, multiple BS can react to the same uncertainty and generate redundant replicas, leading to over-replication. To address this distributed coordination challenge, we propose GATv2-CMASAC, a cooperative multiagent soft actor-critic framework formulated as a Cooperative Partially Observable Stochastic Game (C-POSG). BS agents leverage a dynamic heterogeneous graph enriched with contextaware state representations derived from Graph Attention Transformer v2 (GATv2) embeddings to make informed decisions on task replication and target selection. In addition, we propose a reliability-weighted reward redistribution mechanism that maps global rewards to agent-specific signals using attention coefficients and BS reliability metrics to address credit assignment and delay reduction. Extensive simulations under varying conditions show that GATv2-CMASAC outperforms heuristic and deep-RL baselines, reducing system-wide latency and lowering overreplication while maximizing reliability. Ablation results verify the contributions of GATv2-based representations and reliabilityweighted reward redistribution.

title: Intent-Based Web Application for Managing Sdn Research Clusters.
abstract: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enables flexible, programmable, and vendor-neutral control of network infrastructures. However, operating SDN-based research clusters often requires expert knowledge of low-level interfaces such as the ONOS CLI and REST API, creating a steep learning curve for new users. The Future Computing Group (FCG) at the University of Oulu maintains an SDN-enabled cluster composed of repurposed desktop machines and IoT devices, offering a cost-efficient testbed but lacking intuitive management tools and standardized documentation. This paper presents a systematic exploration of the cluster's architecture and introduces an intentbased web application designed to simplify the management of ONOS controlled research networks. Using network analysis tools such as netcat and tcpdump, we map inter-node communication patterns and document essential operational workflows. We then develop and deploy a web-based interface that leverages the ONOS REST API to enable fine-grained creation, visualization, and control of network intents. Experimental validation confirms that the proposed interface successfully configures host-to-host connectivity and precise flow rules while significantly reducing user effort. This works helps in lowering the entry barrier for researchers and enhance usability without compromising the precision required for SDN experimentation.

title: Distributed Multi-LLM Provenance Graph Construction for Scalable Correlation of APT Logs.
abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) span multiple stages, hosts, and time windows, making end-to-end attack reconstruction from isolated audit events challenging. Provenance graph construction models causal dependencies among system entities; however, in distributed environments, naive event linking produces dense graphs, and centralized analysis scales poorly over large audit logs. This paper presents a multi-LLM framework for provenance graph construction over distributed audit logs. It combines role-specialized agents with Tool-Mediated Context Reduction (TMCR), enabling each agent to access only task-relevant evidence instead of large raw log streams. The framework further incorporates semantic-aware edge selection and anchor-based global correlation to suppress redundant relations and reconstruct cross-host attack paths. Experiments on the APT29 audit-log scenario show that the proposed framework improves edge precision and attack-path reconstruction while significantly reducing graph complexity and token usage compared to single-LLM and multi-LLM baselines without TMCR.

title: SpectralShard: Lightweight Partitioning Under Dynamic Interaction Patterns.
abstract: Distributed computing continuum systems (DCCS) commonly partition application state to enable parallel execution and scale. To avoid costly cross-partition coordination, objects that interact frequently should be assigned to the same partition. Maintaining such efficient partitions under dynamic workloads while keeping updates cheap, however, remains a key challenge. We present SpectralShard, a lightweight partitioning technique based on the spectral structure of the interaction graph. SpectralShard assigns each object a scalar value, derived from a loworder spectral representation of the graph, such that frequently interacting objects receive similar values, and groups objects with nearby values. Because these values can be maintained incrementally as the graph evolves, SpectralShard adapts to workload changes with low overhead, avoiding costly criticalpath computations required by optimization-based approaches. We evaluate SpectralShard on large-scale Ethereum transaction traces as a representative dynamic workload for distributed execution. SpectralShard reduces cross-partition interactions by up to 49.9%, improves throughput by up to 83.5%, and lowers end-to-end latency by up to 38.4% compared to hash-based sharding. These improvements match or exceed those of greedy locality-aware partitioning, while incurring negligible computation on the critical path, comparable to hash-based sharding. Overall, this suggests that low-order spectral methods are a promising building block for adaptive partitioning in DCCS.

title: Towards Semantic-Aware Edge-Cloud Collaboration for Cost-Efficient Video Understanding.
abstract: The proliferation of IoT devices has driven the demand for machine-centric video analytics in vision-critical applications. Unlike human-centric video streaming, these tasks focus on extracting sparse and high-value insights from continuous data streams. To support resource-intensive visual reasoning on constrained edge devices, edge-cloud collaboration is widely adopted. However, existing frameworks face a two-fold challenge. On the edge side, offloading strategies often “blindly” transmit large volumes of redundant background data, overloading network bandwidth and cloud resources. Meanwhile, on the cloud side, resource provisioning faces a fundamental trade-off between minimizing resource costs and ensuring real-time performance under dynamic workloads. To address these challenges, we propose Semantic-aware Edge-cloud Collaboration for cost-efficient video Understanding (SECU), a framework for efficient real-time video analytics. SECU integrates two core components: (1) an edge-side Lightweight Cross-modal Understanding (LCU) module, which distills visual features into semantic keywords to enable selective offloading; and (2) a cloud-side Content Probing-based Optimization (CPO) module, which dynamically requests video content and optimizes cloud resource leasing. This design avoids deploying heavyweight pretrained models on edge devices while enabling scalable and cost-efficient semantic video analytics. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that SECU achieves up to 78.6% cost savings with high semantic accuracy, outperforming existing methods in resource-constrained environments.

title: Coordinating Traffic at Group Granularity for Tail Latency Control in Service Meshes.
abstract: Microservice architectures execute user requests through chains of replica-to-replica remote procedure calls, where end-to-end tail latency is shaped not only by cumulative processing and network delays, but also by how routing decisions are coordinated across replicas at short timescales. Modern service meshes provide a proxy-based data plane for traffic control, yet their default mechanisms expose a fundamental tension: replica-level routing preserves locality and isolation but fragments decisions across many independent proxies, while workload-level proxies improve coordination at the cost of additional inter-node detours and expanded failure domains. Existing heterogeneity-aware schedulers improve long-term traffic distribution by incorporating compute capacity or network latency, but they continue to enforce routing independently at replicas, leaving short-timescale traffic concentration largely unaddressed. As a result, transient queueing and tail-latency spikes persist even under well-provisioned steady-state allocations. We present ARCANE, a traffic control framework that introduces group-level coordination as a new control primitive in service meshes. ARCANE elevates routing decisions from individual replicas to groups of co-located replicas, enabling group-level coordination that mitigates short-timescale traffic concentration while preserving locality and service isolation. ARCANE combines a parameter-free adaptive proportioning algorithm that reacts to runtime load imbalance with a costaware sparse routing construction that reduces routing fragmentation and communication overhead. We implement ARCANE as a Kubernetes operator integrated with Istio and evaluate it on heterogeneous edge–cloud deployments. Experiments on multi-hop service chains demonstrate that ARCANE significantly reduces P99 tail latency and inter-node traffic compared to Least Request, HEART, and Proxy-Service, while remaining compatible with existing service-mesh architectures.

title: VSCI: Verifiable Smooth Coded Inference Via Spline Reconstruction.
abstract: Distributed inference increasingly sits on critical execution paths in decentralized oracle networks, federated clusters, and market-data aggregation fabrics, where outputs must remain available and defensible even when workers are late, missing, or untrusted. In blockchain settings, delayed or incorrect reports can trigger liquidations, settlements, or other state transitions, so distributed availability and verifiable correctness are both first-class requirements. Recent coded-computing methods increasingly provide graceful approximation under stragglers, while recent verifiable-inference systems provide cryptographic, optimistic, or lightweight correctness guarantees. What remains missing is an end-to-end architecture that combines smooth degradation, proof-carrying shard filtering, and a reliability interface that downstream applications can consume. This doctoral research proposes Verifiable Smooth Coded Inference (VSCI), a distributed inference layer that combines learned coded redundancy with proof-carrying verification and reliability-aware aggregation. VSCI encodes an input into$N$shards along a learned one-dimensional trajectory, attaches verifiable execution to each shard, filters invalid shard outputs before aggregation, and reconstructs the final prediction at a fixed anchor using natural cubic spline interpolation. Under a smoothness assumption on the composed function$g=f \circ \gamma$, spline reconstruction yields error that scales as$O\left(h^{4}\right)$in the fill distance of the verified knots, replacing the hard recovery cliff of threshold-based coded schemes with graceful degradation once interpolation is defined. The thesis is that distributed inference systems should provide not only a prediction, but also a correctness-aware and availability-aware reliability signal. To support this goal, VSCI outputs both a decoded prediction and a reliability score that depends on model confidence, verified participation rate, knot geometry, and proof coverage. Current progress establishes the proof-backend side of the system and motivates the next research phase on end-to-end calibration, robustness under missing and Byzantine workers, and the systems trade-off between proof coverage and practical prover cost.

title: Ledgera and its Application to Decentralised Collaborative Fine-Tuning.
abstract: We present Ledgera, a distributed validation and traceability system that enables decentralized applications without relying on global consensus. We demonstrate its use through a collaborative fine-tuning workflow in which multiple stakeholders jointly construct training data and produce machine learning models while retaining control over their contributions. Ledgera provides verifiable execution, cryptographic proofs, and contentbased auditability, allowing all artifacts-from data edits to model checkpoints-to be independently verified. The demo illustrates how decentralized AI workflows can achieve strong guarantees of provenance, accountability, and reproducibility without the overhead of blockchain-based approaches.

title: Trustworthy-PWS: An Operator-Agnostic Public Warning System (PWS) Security Architecture in 5G.
abstract: Public Warning System (PWS), a critical architecture for public safety and emergency alerts through cellular networking, faces a fundamental PWS Trilemma: it must simultaneously ensure universal availability, real-time efficiency, and resilient trust. Current cellular PWS implementations and prior research fail to achieve a balance between these conflicting objectives. Existing research in cellular networking security relies on the mobile network operator to build trust and therefore only works within subscribed network (violating the PWS design goal of universal availability) and becomes ineffective in the presence of the operator's base station's failures (whether due to malicious threat or simply the absence of infrastructure within a given geographic area). To resolve the PWS Trilemma, this study proposes Trustworthy-PWS (T-PWS), a novel operator-agnostic security architecture that decouples alert verification from the mobile network operator. By establishing the public authority (alert initiator) as the independent root of trust and leveraging opportunistic key caching via a secure NAS layer, our architecture enables all users, including roaming and unauthenticated users, to cryptographically verify alerts directly from the public authority, bypassing base stations. To address the strict latency constraints of emergency alerts, we introduce a lightweight commitmentbased protocol using a reverse hash chain that reduces the verification complexity from linear$\mathcal{O}(n)$to a constant$\mathcal{O}(1)$. We validate and evaluate T-PWS with respect to the PWS Trilemma. For resilient trust, we use Tamarin Prover to formally verify the source authentication and resilience against compromised base station infrastructure. For real-time efficiency, we implement T-PWS on a software-defined radio testbed to demonstrate an 85% reduction in cryptographic latency compared to prior research in PWS authentication; For universal availability, we simulate the T-PWS deployment in the US and show that operator-agnostic trust and public key establishment significantly expand geographical coverage, e.g., by more than$9 \%-24 \%$compared to the three major mobile network operators (Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile).

title: FEDLight: A Fuel-Economic Reinforcement Learning Model for Distributed Traffic Signal Control with Spatiotemporal Decomposition.
abstract: This paper addresses the Traffic Signal Control (TSC) problem in urban road networks, where multiple distributed intersections must coordinate their signal scheduling under incomplete observation conditions. As is well known, realworld distributed systems often suffer from partial node failures, sparse sensor deployments, and similar issues, leading to significant information asymmetry across the control network. In TSC systems, these classical problems in distributed systems typically manifest as missing traffic data, which results in inefficient traffic signal control, exacerbating fuel waste through excessive stop-and-go movements and idling. This issue of missing data remains largely unaddressed by most Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods, which generally assume full observability. Moreover, existing approaches that tackle missing data in TSC often overlook the optimization of distributed fuel efficiency. To address the challenges mentioned before and the corresponding fuel consumption issue, this paper proposes a fuel-economic reinforcement learning model for distributed traffic signal control with spatiotemporal decomposition, called FEDLight. Our approach introduces a principled spatiotemporal decomposition mechanism that enables each intersection to locally compute fuel efficiency indicators while preserving global coordination. By integrating an adaptive data imputation module, FEDLight can effectively handle heterogeneous missing data patterns without requiring a centralized data processor. Extensive experiments on large-scale urban traffic networks demonstrate that FEDLight outperforms centralized approaches and other advanced models in reducing fuel consumption while exhibiting strong robustness to varying levels of missing data. This makes it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained distributed environments.

title: ShadowClone: Accelerating Cross-Shard Transactions via Shadow Accounts.
abstract: Sharding is a promising solution to the scalability trilemma in blockchain systems. However, the performance benefits are often offset by the high latency and network congestion associated with cross-shard transactions, which require complex coordination between shards. To address this, we propose ShadowClone, a novel protocol designed to accelerate cross-shard transactions and mitigate congestion. ShadowClone introduces the concept of shadow accounts, allowing the sender's shard to process income operations locally, thereby decoupling the dependency on the receiver's shard for immediate confirmation. To manage the resulting state dispersion, we design a balance reclamation mechanism to recover trapped funds and a dynamic lifetime mechanism to optimize storage overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ShadowClone reduces cross-shard transaction latency by up to 60.4% and increases throughput by 118% compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, it alleviates network congestion by converting 91.9% of cross-shard traffic into intra-shard processing, significantly enhancing overall system efficiency.

title: L-SDFL: A Lightweight Semi-Distributed Federated Learning for Communication Efficiency.
abstract: The proliferation of data volume in the 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems intensifies privacy leakage, making Federated Learning (FL) a critical privacy-preserving solution for decentralized model training by keeping raw data on local devices while aggregating only model parameters. While Distributed and Semi-Distributed FL (D/SD-FL) overcome the single-point failures and scalability limits of centralized FL, they introduce significant communication and computational overheads due to extensive peer-to-peer exchanges and consensus mechanisms. In this paper, we propose L-SDFL, a Lightweight SDFL framework with efficient temporary aggregator election and model optimization schemes to balance performance with resource efficiency. L-SDFL integrates a distributed Pruning-based Local Model optimization scheme (PLM), two aggregator evaluation schemes (AEA and AET), and a Pruning-based Global Model aggregation scheme (PGM). Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed L-SDFL outperforms existing algorithms in key performance metrics, such as communication cost, computational cost, and model accuracy.

title: Congestion Adaptive Load Balancing with in-Network Reordering for Datacenter Networks.
abstract: With the rapid expansion of link capacity and the increasing performance requirements of emerging applications and services, modern data center networks have widely deployed Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) to deliver ultra-low latency and high throughput. However, existing load balancing solutions either suffer from packet loss due to the limitation of hardware resources in RDMA network interface cards, or are far from optimal for mixed-flow parallel transmission. In this paper, we propose a congestion adaptive load balancing with in-network reordering, called CALB, to guarantee that packets arrive at the receiver without reordering, thereby minimizing flow completion time as well as the deadline miss rate. The key idea is that CALB periodically inspects the congestion status of each path while measuring its available bandwidth. Once a flow experiences congestion or one deadline flow may fail to finish transmission within its deadline, the switch assigns one path with available bandwidth matching the congested flow's. Moreover, CALB employs an in-network reordering mechanism to ensure packets arrive at the receiver in order. The evaluation results demonstrate that CALB can reduce deadline miss rate by up to 85% and the flow completion time by up to 65% compared with the state-of-the-art load balancing solutions.

title: Fafnir: A Flexible Load Generator for Reproducible ML Inference Benchmarks.
abstract: Systems research on machine learning (ML) inference servers is an emerging field, often dependent on benchmarking. Research, however, lacks an easy-to-use yet flexible tool to benchmark and compare innovative inference systems with existing solutions. As a consequence, inference systems under test (SUTs) and benchmarks are often tightly coupled. We propose Fafnir, a benchmarking tool to overcome this tight coupling, making different SUTs comparable and benchmark results reproducible. Our demonstrator shows that Fafnir is easy to use yet flexible enough to benchmark complex scenarios in addition to standard scenarios that involve, for example, commonly used Poisson or fixed interarrival time request distributions.

title: Providing Cross-Chain Interoperability Through Decentralized Message Routing and Delivery.
abstract: The increasing demand for blockchain applications has led to a surge of new public blockchains to support this growth. However, the availability of additional blockchains also fragments liquidity and, forces users into transacting on unfamiliar chains and protocols in order to address this fragmentation which potentially increases a user's exposure to risks. This creates a challenging user experience especially for the new users that are driving the increasing demand. Cross-chain communication can tackle this issue by providing interoperability for smart contracts across blockchains. However, current cross-chain delivery solutions either only support message passing between directly connected chains, which significantly limits their connectivity, or are centralized, requiring messages to be routed through a single hub chain. In this paper, we show that inter-blockchain communication can become more robust and efficient by leveraging wellunderstood concepts from traditional communication networks such as routing, name resolution, and policy-based message delivery. We introduce Baton, a secure routing and message delivery framework that consists of (1) Baton Core, a collection of modules that enable policy-driven multi-hop messaging; and (2) Relayer Network, a network of relayers that are incentivized to collaboratively route and deliver messages. Our experimental results demonstrate a higher degree of decentralization and enhanced scalability compared to existing solutions that connect blockchains in hub-and-spoke topologies, particularly under heavy network loads.

title: ZeroTrustNet: A Software-Defined Perimeter Framework with Decentralised Identifiers for Zero Trust Network Security.
abstract: This paper presents an unified framework for the practical adoption of Zero Trust security principles in distributed network environments. The proposed ZeroTrustNet architecture integrates three tightly coupled components: a Zero Trust policy engine that enforces continuous authentication and fine-grained authorization for every network interaction; a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) control plane built on the Ryu Pythonbased controller, which enables dynamic and programmable flow management; and a decentralized identity layer grounded in Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), which assigns verifiable and persistent identities to all network nodes. Deployed and evaluated within a Mininet-based emulation environment, the framework intercepts network traffic in real time, verifies node credentials against predefined Zero Trust policies, and dynamically installs flow rules to isolate suspicious entities. Experimental results demonstrate that, whereas a traditional network allows a single compromised node to propagate an attack across the entire infrastructure, the proposed architecture confines the impact to exactly one node regardless of network scale. These findings confirm the scalability and resilience of the ZeroTrustNet framework for securing modern distributed networks.

title: CAED: Context-Aware Data Cleaning Tool.
abstract: Detecting erroneous values in tabular datasets remains one of the most important, challenging, and time-consuming tasks. It is crucial to maintain high-quality data for better analysis and accurate decision-making. However, the task is complex due to the different types of errors that could occur in each dataset such as typos, outliers, inconsistencies, and outof-domain values. These errors can be classified into syntax-based errors where erroneous values do not conform to the structure or domain of the attribute, and semantic errors, where values are syntactically correct but do not fit the context. The various contexts in which these errors occur make it hard to design a tool to detect all errors in all contexts. In this research, we developed a tool that uses the context-awareness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform context-aware error detection of semantic and syntactic errors. By profiling the datasets to optimize the size and quality of provided input to the LLMs and employing prompt engineering designed for error detection, our tool is capable of detecting errors that cannot be detected with other error detection tools.

title: Interactive Demonstration of Asynchronous Quantum-as-a-Service for Autonomous Driving.
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are an emerging option for autonomous vehicle perception, but their high inference latency makes direct real-time deployment challenging. We present AQUAD, an asynchronous vehicle-to-edge (V2E) framework that integrates a slow quantum perception model into a fast onboard pipeline without blocking local execution. AQUAD combines adaptive offloading with asynchronous quality rescue, allowing delayed edge results to refine ongoing classical perception while preserving responsiveness. We implement AQUAD using PyTorch, TorchQuantum, and multithreaded Python, and demonstrate it on the KITTI dataset through an interactive dashboard showing real-time detections, bird's-eye-view projections, latency, communication overhead, and rescue events. The demo illustrates the feasibility of asynchronous quantum-assisted edge intelligence for real-time autonomous driving.

title: SplitQ-PEFT: Quantum-Enhanced PEFT for Communication-Efficient Split Learning.
abstract: Split learning offers a practical framework for privacy-aware distributed training, but adapting large language models in such settings still requires substantial communication and optimization cost. We propose SplitQ-PEFT, a quantumenhanced PEFT framework for communication-efficient split learning. By introducing compact quantum-smashed representations, SplitQ-PEFT significantly reduces the per-step communication overhead while retaining competitive adaptation performance. Across multiple benchmarks, SplitQ-PEFT requires the fewest trainable parameters and achieves the lowest communication overhead among the compared PEFT baselines, while maintaining competitive performance on generative tasks. Further entropy and visualization analyses show that the quantumsmashed representation remains compact yet expressive. Our results suggest that SplitQ-PEFT is an effective approach for communication-efficient and parameter-efficient LLM adaptation in split learning environments.

title: SpecPool: Storage-Layer Speculation for Parallel Smart Contract Execution.
abstract: Modern blockchains face execution bottlenecks as rising transaction loads exceed the limits of sequential processing, threatening scalability. Exploiting parallelism safely, while preserving determinism, is essential to address this challenge. SpecPool transforms the blockchain mempool-traditionally a passive queue-into an active preprocessing engine. While transactions await consensus, SpecPool predicts a likely block execution order using mempool-visible signals such as fees, arrival time, and coarse batching windows while respecting persender nonce ordering. It then predicts potential conflicts between transactions by combining static analysis of contract bytecode with historical access patterns. Transactions are subsequently speculatively pre-executed in parallel according to the predicted order within sandboxed environments, extracting transaction read/write sets and invocation chains. This metadata enables conflict-aware validation, maximizing concurrency while preserving consensus-consistent ordering. Operating at the storage layer, SpecPool requires no modifications to virtual machine semantics or consensus protocols, simplifying adoption in existing blockchain systems. We implement SpecPool in the Cosmos framework and evaluate it using workloads derived from the Injective blockchain. Experiments demonstrate up to a$60 \times$reduction in block validation latency and 20% throughput improvement over prior parallel execution approaches. We additionally analyze the effects of block predictability and transaction mempool visibility in a high-frequency blockchain, showing that SpecPool maintains accurate order prediction and effective parallelism even under Injective's block time of 0.63 seconds.
